Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Review the terms used for groin pain syndromes
Differentiate athletic pubalgia and core muscle injury from intra-articular hip pathology.
Identify potential pathologies contributing to groin pain syndromes.
Identify treatment methods for athletic pubalgia and core muscle injuries.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Common names: sports hernia, sportsman groin, athletic pubalgia, Gilmore groin, incipient
hernia, core muscle injury, inguinal disruption, adductor-related groin pain

Extra-articular groin pain that may be isolated or occur in combination with intra-articular hip


Overview
Athletic pubalgia, sports hernia, and core muscle injuries are common causes of extra-
articular hip and groin pain, especially in the athletic population. Despite the frequency
of these injuries, they are poorly understood by the medical community. Reasons for this
poor understanding include the lack of a well-described mechanism for the pathology,
varied nomenclature, and the pathology being managed by multiple medical specialties.
Many terms are used to describe this category of injuries, including sports hernia,
sportsman groin, athletic pubalgia, Gilmore groin, incipient hernia, core muscle injury,
adductor-related groin pain, and inguinal disruption (Resource 1) Given the many
different terms and their somewhat misleading nature, we refer to this category of
injuries as groin pain syndromes.
Epidemiology
Approximately 6% of all athletic injuries (Resource 2)
Professional and amateur athletes susceptible

Epidemiology
Groin pain syndrome can present in the average population but is more common in the
athletic population, with one study reporting that 82% of patients with groin pain
syndrome were athletes. Athletes involved in cutting and pivoting sports appear to be
most susceptible because of sudden and repetitive high loads placed across the core
and adductor musculature.
Anatomy and Biomechanics


Anatomy and Biomechanics
The anterior pelvis and hip bony anatomy work in intricate concert with the musculature
of the abdominal wall and thigh. Groin pain has previously been described in three
anatomic locations: anterior (abdominal musculature, sartorius, iliacus, psoas, pectineus,
quadriceps muscles), medial (adductor muscles, gracilis, obturator externus), and
posterior (hamstrings and portion of the adductor magnus). The layer concept is another
method to categorize pathology into four distinct layers: (1) osseus layer, (2) inert tissue
layer, (3) contractile layer, (4) neurovascular layer.1 Better understanding of the potential
pathology in each layer allows for the better diagnosis and management of injuries in
this complex anatomic region (Figure 1).
The pubis serves as the focal point of the groin musculature, balancing the forces at the
hip joint, pubic symphysis, abdominal muscles, and adductors. The pubic aponeurosis,
which consists of the rectus abdominis, conjoint tendon (internal oblique and
transversus abdominis), and external oblique, inserts on the pubic tubercle and exerts a
superior force. The medial thigh and adductor muscles, consisting of the gracilis,
pectineus, adductor brevis, adductor longus, and adductor magnus muscles, originate
on the pubis and exert an inferior and lateral vector. These forces coalesce at the pubis
and result in a large amount of torque on the pubic symphysis.

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Pain in the inguinal region without a frank hernia
Imbalance of forces acting on the pubis
Often the result of overuse and may be exacerbated by hip impingement or restricted range of


Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Groin pain syndrome is pain in the inguinal region, typically in an athlete, without an
overt hernia. Although a common alternative term is sports hernia, this is misleading
because no hernia is present. Groin pain syndrome may be caused by various discreet
pathologies. These include rectus abdominus insertion tearing or abnormalities; tearing
or attenuation of the transversalis fascia or conjoint tendon; partial avulsion of the
internal oblique muscle fibers at their insertion on the pubic tubercle; tearing of the
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:25 AM
AAOS | Athletic Pubalgia and Core Muscle Injury
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000045
5/24

internal or external oblique musculature or aponeurosis; weakening of the inguinal ring;
and tendinitis or partial tearing of the adductor muscle group at its origin, commonly the
adductor longus.2
The pubis is the nexus of multiple forces across the anterior hip and, therefore, is
integral in the development of groin pain syndrome. The superiorly directed forces of
the core musculature work against the inferiorly directed forces of the adductors. If
acting in harmony, these muscles stabilize the core and act as shock absorbers for the
symphysis.
If these antagonistic forces are not balanced, pathologic changes to the musculature and
instability of the symphysis can result over time, resulting in considerable pain in this
region. These changes are particularly prevalent in patients who participate in athletic
activities because of the extreme torque exerted through rapid muscle contraction.
Under-strengthening or poor conditioning of one muscle group in combination with
incoordination and inflexibility may exacerbate stresses. An imbalance in opposing
forces will not only be transmitted across the symphysis but also create strain on the
inguinal tissues, leading to weakening of the inguinal ring and fascia.
Intra-articular hip pathology commonly coexists with groin pathology. Often, this is a
related finding because hip impingement restricts range of motion, further altering
biomechanics and transferring motion and stress elsewhere in the region. Although
these forces are dissipated in the inguinal structures, the hip capsule and labrum likely
help in absorption, leading to labral tears over time.
Risk Factors
Sports with high levels of cutting and pivoting
Inadequate conditioning and flexibility
Femoroacetabular impingement (FAI)
Associated Injuries
FAI
SEND FEEDBACK

6/24


Associated Injuries
Athletes may have multiple etiologies contributing to their symptoms. FAI often coexists
with groin pain syndrome, with radiographic evidence in up to 86% of patients.3
Decreased hip range of motion in patients with FAI requires compensation from
elsewhere around the hip, leading to increased range of motion and stress across the
pubic symphysis and the surrounding musculature.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
History
Patients report deep groin or abdominal pain, which may vary from bothersome to
debilitating.
Pain may radiate into the testicular region, perineum, or medial thigh.
Symptoms usually are of an insidious onset, but patients may be able to pinpoint a specific
instance of a popping or tearing sensation.
Typically, pain is worse with activity, especially sudden changes of direction, acceleration,
cutting, twisting, sprinting, or lateral movements.
Pain may be exacerbated by Valsalva maneuvers, such as with coughing, sneezing, or bowel
movements.

History
Patients usually describe a deep inguinal or low abdominal pain that has insidiously
worsened over time; however, a specific inciting event may be noted (eg, while kicking a
soccer ball or making a hard cut). The pain is usually worsened by athletic movements
with quick acceleration or change of direction and activities that involve a Valsalva
maneuver, such as coughing, sneezing, or bearing down with a bowel movement. Rest
usually helps; however, the pain may worsen after the patient sits for extended periods
and when he or she gets into and out of bed or a car. If the adductor tendons are
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:25 AM
AAOS | Athletic Pubalgia and Core Muscle Injury
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000045
7/24

involved, the patient may describe pain that radiates down the medial thigh with active
adduction of the leg (Resource 3).
Physical Examination
Tenderness to palpation over the pubic tubercle, lower rectus abdominis, or adductor tendons
Pain with resisted sit-up and leg adduction
Thorough regional examination to rule out concomitant pathology

Physical Examination
A key aspect of the physical examination is palpation of the pubic tubercle, pubic
symphysis, adductor muscles origin, lower rectus abdominis, internal and external
oblique muscles, and the inguinal ring for tenderness. Pain in these areas may be
exacerbated by resisted sit-up with the hips extended and the ipsilateral hip crossed
over in a figure-of-4 position or by the external rotation Stinchfield test.4 Combining
resisted adduction with palpation may increase sensitivity for adductor pathology. With
the patient in the supine position, the feet are placed flat on the examination table with
the hips and knees flexed. The provider’s forearm is placed between the patient’s knees,
with the palm resisting adduction of one hip while the distal arm resists the other hip.
This allows a free hand to palpate the adductor tendon to evaluate for tenderness.
A regional examination also is important to diagnose concomitant pathology. Hips
should be taken through range of motion and impingement and evaluated via the FADIR
(flexion, adduction, internal rotation) and FABER (flexion, abduction, external rotation)
tests. Assessment of the gluteal tendons, trochanteric bursa, sacroiliac joints, and
lumbar spine should be performed, and the patient should be examined in the supine
and standing positions to evaluate for femoral or inguinal hernias.
Imaging Studies
Radiography

AP pelvis and lateral hip radiographs

Radiography
Imaging should begin with AP pelvis and modified Dunn lateral hip radiographs.
Typically, these radiographs are negative but are used to rule out bony hip impingement,
avulsion fractures, stress fractures, osteitis pubis, sacralized lumbar vertebrae, or tumor
as a source of pain. If the pubic symphysis is involved, sclerosis or widening caused by
bone resorption may be observed.2
Computed Tomography
Typically, CT is not performed unless necessary to further investigate pathology detected on
radiographs.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Preferred imaging modality
Dedicated athletic pubalgia protocol

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Currently, MRI is the preferred imaging modality to evaluate patients with groin pain. A
dedicated athletic pubalgia protocol should be used, which includes a large and small
field-of-view sequence focused on the pubic symphysis.5 The most common MRI finding
of groin pain syndrome is fluid signal extending from the anterior-inferior rectus
abdominis insertion to the adductor tendons origin on sagittal or axial MRIs. Osteitis
pubis is indicated by symmetric bone marrow edema of the pubic bones or fluid in the
symphysis and surrounding soft tissues. MRI is associated with a sensitivity and
specificity as high as 68% and 100%, respectively, for the detection of rectus abdominis
tendinopathy, and a sensitivity and specificity as high as 86% and 89%, respectively, for

femoral hernias (Figure 2).

abdominal and proximal adductor-related pain shows disruption of the distal rectus
abdominis/adductor aponeurosis on the left (arrow). (Reproduced with permission from

Bone Scintigraphy

Bone Scintigraphy

Technetium Tc-99m bone scintigraphy can detect pathology in the superior pubis, pubic
symphysis, and adductor tendon origin. Technetium Tc-99m bone scintigraphy can help
rule out osteitis pubis, symphyseal instability, tumor, and osteoarthritis. Given the
widespread use of MRI, technetium Tc-99m bone scintigraphy affords little added benefit
but with the added risk of radiation exposure.
Ultrasonography
Dynamic ultrasonography affords visualization of the inguinal canal. Although ultrasonography
is vulnerable to operator error, dynamic ultrasonography may afford cost-efficient, real-time
imaging of the inguinal canal.

Differential Diagnosis

The differential diagnosis for groin pain syndrome is vast and spans multiple body
systems. This highlights the importance of an in-depth knowledge of anatomy and a
thorough physical examination and clinical history to narrow the list of potential
diagnoses. Multiple pathologies, such as core muscle injury and associated intra-articular
hip pathology, may exist concurrently.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Indications
First-line treatment for initial presentation of groin pain syndrome

Indications
A course of nonsurgical treatment should be attempted in athletes presenting with groin
pain before considering surgical treatment. Acute injuries from a defined event generally
subside with rest.7 Often, patients do not present in an acute setting and will not see a
sports medicine physician until the pain has become chronic. Some surgeons believe
that chronic groin pain syndrome is less likely to respond to nonsurgical management;
however, this has not been well studied (Resources 4 and 5).
Techniques/Procedures
Rest
Physical therapy
NSAIDs
Injections

Techniques/Procedures
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:25 AM
AAOS | Athletic Pubalgia and Core Muscle Injury
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000045
13/24

Most groin pain syndromes will resolve with rest and the avoidance of provocative
activities. NSAIDs may be a beneficial adjuvant treatment option to decrease swelling
and pain. Physical therapy is a mainstay of management, especially if the pain has
become chronic.7 The first 2 weeks of treatment are primarily focused on stretching,
whereas later physical therapy addresses core strengthening and decreasing muscle
imbalances in the hip and pelvic stabilizers. If substantial improvement is achieved, then
sport-specific activities are introduced. Physical therapy often is performed for 3 months,
and athletes who are pain-free at 10 to12 weeks can return to sports activity at that time.
If no improvement is made after 3 months of physical therapy, then surgical treatment
may be considered.
Injections can be used for management but also are beneficial in the diagnosis of groin
pain syndrome. Often, the diagnosis is not clear or intra-articular pathology obscures the
clinical picture. Local anesthetic agents, with or without steroids, can be injected in the
region in which pathology is suspected to determine if symptoms improve. These
regions include the hip joint, adductor tendon origin, pubic symphysis, and psoas
tendon. After the anesthetic agent has had time to take effect, the patient can be asked
to perform tasks that would normally provoke pain to determine if the pain generator
was the focus of the injection. If this is not helpful, then local anesthetic agents can be
injected into another area.
Surgical Management
Indications
Failure of at least 6 to 12 weeks of nonsurgical management, including physical therapy
Positive diagnostic injection
High-level athlete wishing to quickly return to sports activity, depending on timing within the
season
Combined groin pain syndrome and FAI

Indications
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:25 AM
AAOS | Athletic Pubalgia and Core Muscle Injury
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000045
14/24

In general, patients should complete an adequate trial of nonsurgical treatment (at least
6 weeks; often 3 months), before surgical treatment is considered. If diagnostic
injections indicate an identifiable groin pathology, the surgeon may be more confident
that groin surgery may be helpful. The treatment plan is tailored to the specific patient.
Earlier surgical treatment, without a full trial of nonsurgical treatment, can be discussed
with high-level athletes if a quicker return to play is important, depending on the timing
within the sports season.
A subset of patients will present with overlapping groin pain and symptoms of FAI. This is
not uncommon, and more recent studies have reported that FAI results in abnormal
motion and increases strain on the symphysis, predisposing patients to athletic pubalgia.
Approximately 50% of athletes with groin pain syndrome are thought to have a labral
tear, and 86% of athletes with groin pain syndrome have FAI observed on radiographs.8
If the patient history, physical examination, and imaging studies suggest combined
pathology, diagnostic injections are especially useful to help delineate the level of
discomfort from each entity. If the physician believes that both pathologies are
considerable contributors to pain, then both pathologies should be managed surgically
because addressing only one pathology likely will result in an inferior outcome. In a
study of patients with FAI and athletic pubalgia, the patients who underwent groin
surgery alone returned to their previous level of sports activity 25% of the time. The
patients who underwent hip arthroscopy for the management of FAI alone returned to
their previous level of sports activity 50% of the time. The patients who underwent
combined surgical treatment returned to their previous level of sports activity 85% to
91% of the time. Performing the surgical procedures in a staged fashion or in a single
setting did not affect patient outcomes.6
Contraindications
Unclear diagnosis
Improvement with nonsurgical management
Techniques/Procedures
Preoperative Planning

9/3/26, 7:25 AM
AAOS | Athletic Pubalgia and Core Muscle Injury
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000045
15/24

Referral to general surgeon experienced in groin/hernia surgery
If concurrent intra-articular hip pathology, single setting versus staged procedure

Preoperative Planning
Patients with groin pain syndrome who require surgical fixation should be referred to a
general surgeon with experience in athletic pubalgia and hernia surgery because this
type of procedure typically is outside the scope of orthopaedic practice. If the patient
also has FAI and has elected to undergo hip arthroscopy, this can be scheduled as a
combined procedure or as two anesthetic events. Performing surgical procedures in a
staged fashion or in a single setting does not result in a difference in patient outcomes,
and the choice depends on surgeon availability and patient preference.4
Patient Positioning
Supine
Standard surgical table or bed with hip arthroscopy attachment (if both procedures performed
during one anesthetic event)
Surgical Approaches
Many described techniques, with none proven to be superior
Goals
Relieve force on the pubic joint by altering unequal tension
Reinforce weak structures or defects
Neurectomy or nerve decompression as needed
Determine
Open or minimally invasive approach
Mesh or no mesh
Adductor longus involvement
Open repairs without mesh: Typically, these repairs involve an inguinal incision similar to a
procedure for an inguinal hernia repair. They allow for great exposure of the inguinal canal
down to the adductor longus insertion on the pubis.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:25 AM
AAOS | Athletic Pubalgia and Core Muscle Injury
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000045
16/24

Gilmore technique: Gilmore popularized a modification of the Nesovic approach for Bassini
suture repair. Nesovic and Bassini described disruption of the external oblique, conjoint
tendon, and inguinal ligament, resulting in nerve compression from a weakened inguinal
canal floor. Gilmore discusses the use of an absorbable suture to repair a defect in the
transversus abdominis or the internal oblique, followed by nylon suture repair of the internal
oblique to the inguinal ligament, to change the vector of pull of muscles and ligaments and
decompress the nerves.9 Twenty percent of the patients in the series by Gilmore also had an
adductor longus tenotomy.
Meyers technique: Meyers performed a large case series but did not provide in-depth detail
on his technique.10 What can be inferred is that Meyers repaired the rectus abdominis fascia
to the pubis and the medial inguinal ligament and opened the adductor longus fascia,
suturing this cranially to reinforce the rectus repair. The Meyers technique also included
division of the superficial inguinal canal nerves and longitudinal incisions in the longus to
promote healing.
Muschaweck technique: Common pathologic findings Muschaweck describes include medial
displacement of the rectus and weaking of the inguinal floor.11 Muschaweck promotes
opening the transversalis fascia and repairing it in two layers in a vest-over-pants fashion to
reinforce the floor and reduce weakness. The sutures also are fixed on the pubic tubercle to
attempt to slightly lateralize the rectus to change the vector of pull. The genitofemoral nerve
is transected in a minority of patients.
Mesh repairs, open: Open mesh repairs typically are a variation of the Lichtenstein technique
for repair. Various physicians have reportedly performed this type of procedure.
Campanelli technique: Campanelli has been a proponent of open repair with mesh.12
Campanelli typically describes the pathology as weakening of the inguinal floor, hypertrophy
of the rectus and adductor longus, and subsequent compression of the inguinal nerves. This
repair involves the use of mesh to reinforce the inguinal floor, partial rectus and adductor
tenotomy, and transection of all three inguinal sensory nerves.
Minimally invasive mesh repairs: These repair techniques involve the use of a transabdominal
preperitoneal or a totally extraperitoneal approach.8 The totally extraperitoneal approach is
the same as that used for inguinal hernia repair. These repairs commonly reinforce defects but
do not directly decompress nerves; however, hypothetically reinforcing weak spots would
prevent bowstringing of the nerve in the Hesselbach triangle and, thus, relieve pressure. Meta-
analyses have reported patient outcomes similar to those of open procedures, with earlier
return to the sports activity. Disadvantages of minimally invasive repair include a steeper
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:25 AM
AAOS | Athletic Pubalgia and Core Muscle Injury
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000045
17/24

learning curve, dependence on the use of mesh, the need for general anesthesia, slightly
higher complication rate, and inability to visualize anterior structures for direct decompression
or repair. Because of the inability to visualize and decompress the ilioinguinal nerve, some
studies recommend against minimally invasive approaches if a patient reports symptoms of
neuralgia.
Paajanen technique: In 2004, Paajanen conducted an early series that included 41 patients.13
The authors of the study reported conjoint tendon tears in 25% of the patients, muscle
asymmetry in 17% of the patients, and no abnormalities in approximately 50% of the
patients. The authors performed totally extraperitoneal repair with mesh and adductor
tenotomy in two patients. Short-term outcomes were good. Subsequently, other studies have
reported similar outcomes with transabdominal preperitoneal and totally extraperitoneal
repair with or without adductor tenotomy.
Lloyd release technique: Lloyd believed the underlying problem was inguinal ligament
tension on the pubis.14 The authors used a transabdominal preperitoneal approach to
laparoscopically release the inguinal ligament from the pubic tubercle to relieve tension and
provided reinforcement with the use of mesh.
Adductor longus surgery: Adductor longus tendinopathy is thought to be a source of pain in
many athletes. The imbalance in tension from the relatively stronger longus over the weaker
rectus abdominis is thought to be a major contributor to the pathophysiology of groin pain
syndrome.8
Adductor longus tenotomy: Complete tenotomy can be performed in isolation or as an
adjunct procedure. The tendon can be approached through the inguinal incision during an
open procedure or through a separate incision over the longus tendon, approximately 1 cm
inferior to the groin crease if performed during minimally invasive repair or as a separate
procedure. The epimysia (fascia) over the tendon is incised, the tendon is isolated with the
use of a clamp, and the tendon is divided via electrocautery. This will theoretically change the
vector of pull on the pubis, relieve pressure, and decompress the obturator nerve.
Partial adductor longus tenotomy: Partial release or fractional lengthening can be
performed; however, this technique should be used with caution in soccer players because it
may lead to striking weakness.6
Adductor longus repair: Repair of full-thickness adductor longus ruptures to the pubic bone
with the use of suture anchors has been described. In a series of National Football League
athletes with full-thickness longus tears, no strength deficits were noted in those who
underwent repair versus those who were treated nonsurgically. The patients in the
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:25 AM
AAOS | Athletic Pubalgia and Core Muscle Injury
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000045
18/24

nonsurgical group returned to play at 6 weeks, whereas the patients in the surgical group
returned to play at 12 weeks.6
Senior author’s preferred technique: Although each patient and each pathology are unique,
the approach currently used by the senior author includes:
Open inguinal incision
Neurectomy of the entrapped nerve (usually sparing the iliohypogastric)
Reinforcement and lateralization of the rectus abdominis
Full-thickness adductor longus tenotomy if adductor symptoms are present

Surgical Approaches
Many surgical techniques have been developed to manage groin pain syndrome.
Although large series and meta-analyses have been performed, no well-controlled trials
have reported the efficacy of one technique over another. The general principles of
these procedures are to balance force on the pubic joint from unequal torque, reinforce
weakened structures or fascial defects, and address damaged sensory nerves via
decompression or neurectomy. The 2014 Manchester Consensus Conference released
the following statement: “The surgery itself relies on identifying pathology, releasing any
abnormal tension and restoring anatomy with suture or mesh reinforcement. There is
no evidence from [randomized controlled trials] ... to support the superiority of any type
of operation.”1 An overview of the most commonly described surgical techniques is
provided (Figure 3).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:25 AM

Figure 3 Illustrations show the surgical management of groin pain syndrome. A,
Illustration shows the normal anatomy of the inguinal canal and pubic joint. The external
oblique (EO) fascia is opened through the external ring, exposing the floor of the inguinal
canal, with the spermatic cord (SC) retracted laterally. The rectus abdominis (RA) tendon
inserts onto the pubic bone from above, meeting the tendinous insertion of the
adductor longus (AL) muscle to form a common enthesial plate. B, Illustration shows the
modified Bassini or Gilmore repair technique. Sutured tissue repairs reinforce the
inguinal floor and the direct space. C, Illustration shows the Muschaweck technique. A
weakness in the inguinal canal floor is repaired with minimal tension by opening the
transversalis fascia and performing sutured plication repair to decompress the
genitofemoral nerve. The RA also is slightly lateralized. D, Illustration shows adductor
longus tenotomy. A full tenotomy involves opening the overlying epimysia and cutting
the tendon and the lateral muscular portion attaching to the pubic bone. Partial
tenotomies also can be performed. E, Illustration shows the Meyer technique. The rectus
muscle is reinforced to the pubic bone and slightly lateralized on the inguinal ligament.
In addition, complete epimysiotomy and freeing of the AL tendon without tenotomy are
performed, and the epimysia is sutured cranially to the enthesial plate. Multiple, small
longitudinal slits are made to promote neovascularization and minimal lengthening.
(Reproduced with permission from Zuckerbraun BS, Cyr AR, Mauro CS: Groin pain
syndrome known as sports hernia: A review. JAMA Surg 2020;155[4]:340–348.)

Complications
Edema
The most common postoperative complication is edema in the perineum, thighs, abdomen, or
genitalia.15
Infection
Wound infection is reported in approximately 0.4% of patients.15
Hematoma
Hematoma requiring revision surgery is reported in 0.3% of patients.15
Neural Injury/Nerve Palsy
Nerve dysesthesia occurs in less than 1% of patients and most commonly involves the
anterior/lateral femoral cutaneous nerve, ilioinguinal nerve, and genitofemoral nerve
distributions.15
Revision Surgery
The most common cause of revision surgery is groin pain syndrome on the contralateral side.
Inadequate adductor release or repair at the time of surgery may require revision surgery.
Not addressing FAI at the time of surgery will likely lead to continued disability and the need
for subsequent surgical management.

With open techniques, 95% of patients return to sports activity 3 months postoperative.8
Large case series have reported success rates ranging from 85% to 100% in patients who
undergo surgical treatment.8,15
The follow-up duration of series ranges from 6 weeks to 5 years. Longer follow-up is necessary
to determine recurrence after return to full activity and sports activity for a prolonged period.
In a study of 100 athletes with a rectus abdominus adductor longus aponeurotic plate injury
who underwent repair, Emblom et al16 reported that 98% returned to sport.
